title: Application Layer Protocol: Publish/Subscribe Protocols
summary: Publish and subscribe protocols give an attacker a message broker as a middle layer, so the malware never speaks directly to attacker infrastructure. Under the application layer protocol parent technique, this sub-technique covers the broker based protocols such as Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT), Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP), Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP), and Simple Text Oriented Messaging Protocol (STOMP), where publishers post messages to named topics and subscribers receive whatever matches their subscriptions. An implant connects to a broker, subscribes to a topic that the operator controls, and reads commands from the message payload; results are published to another topic. Because the connection is a single steady client to broker session, the network view shows ordinary application traffic, and on internal deployments it may never cross the perimeter at all. Broker visibility is therefore the priority control: authentication and authorisation on the broker, logging of topic subscriptions and publishes, and inventory of which internal devices run a broker. Detection signals include clients with no matching business function, topics whose names do not follow the normal naming scheme, payloads containing encoded or executable content, connection patterns at fixed intervals, and unidentified devices reaching a cloud broker over an encrypted web port.

beginner.definition: This is when malware talks to a message broker instead of to the attacker directly. Users post messages to a topic and others read the topics they follow. The malware reads its orders from a topic and posts answers back.
beginner.whyItMatters: A broker hides the attacker. The victim machine only ever talks to one server, which might be a normal service inside your company. Blocking the attacker's address is not enough, because the attacker never connects to the victim.
howItWorks: Publish and subscribe systems use a central broker that passes messages between clients.
Each message belongs to a topic, which is a named channel such as a room in a chat system.
Clients subscribe to the topics they care about and the broker sends them matching messages.
Malware connects to a broker, subscribes to a topic the attacker chose, and waits for instructions.
The attacker publishes a command to that topic, and the malware publishes the results to another topic.
Every connection looks like a normal application talking to a normal service, so it blends in well.
beginner.example: Picture the notice board in a shared flat. Anyone can pin a note to a labelled section, and only the people who follow that section read it. The person who pinned the note never had to meet anyone. The board itself saw only ordinary notes.
takeaways: Publish and subscribe traffic is client to broker, so the attacker's address is not in the connection.
Unusual topic names and encoded payloads inside messages are the strongest clues.
If you run a broker, enable authentication and log subscriptions and published messages.

objectives: Explain how publish and subscribe protocols differ from direct client to server communication.
Describe the roles of the broker, the publisher, and the subscriber.
Name common publish and subscribe protocols and where they are normally used.
Explain why blocking attacker addresses does not stop this command channel.
Identify the broker logs and network telemetry that reveal malicious use.
